summary: A summary index of RFCs numbered 1800 through 1899, listing them for readers who want to find what was published in that range. It is an informational list, not a protocol description.

plainLanguage.summary: This is like a table of contents for a shelf of one hundred notes, so you can find the one you want.

subtitle: An index of 100 RFC documents covering the decade's worth of Internet work.

tldr.problem: The RFC series was growing large; finding relevant documents in the 1800-1899 range was difficult without a summary.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1899 lists each of the 100 RFCs in this range with a one-line or short-paragraph description of its topic and status.
tldr.outcome: This became a standard reference for learning what was published during this period of rapid Internet development.

today: RFC 1899 is an informational summary with no standards content. It stands as a historical document capturing the state of Internet protocol work in the mid-1990s. It has been superseded by later summary RFCs covering subsequent RFC ranges.

sections.title: A Snapshot of Internet Work 1995-1997
sections.content:
RFC 1899 is a summary and index of Request for Comments documents numbered 1800 through 1899, published between June 1995 and January 1997. This period saw intense development in several areas: the transition toward IPv6, the consolidation of Internet security protocols, the standardization of MIME and email extensions, and the emergence of web technologies like HTML 2.0. The index briefly describes each RFC's title and purpose, allowing readers to navigate this diverse set of documents.

The memo notes that many RFCs in this range were on the standards track, meaning they were being evaluated for potential adoption as Internet standards. For the precise status of each, readers were directed to the latest edition of the Internet Official Protocol Standards document.
sections.plainLanguage: During these two years, the Internet grew fast. New protocols for video, email, and the next version of IP were being written. This document is a table of contents for all of them.

sections.title: Major Topics Covered
sections.content: The RFCs numbered 1800-1899 span several major areas. IPv6 and addressing dominated this range: RFC 1883 (IPv6 specification), RFC 1885 (ICMPv6), RFC 1886 (DNS for IPv6), and several others defining the architecture and allocation of IPv6 addresses. Security and cryptography formed another large group, including IP authentication headers, encryption protocols, and key exchange mechanisms. Email and MIME extensions proliferated, with new content types for enriched text, CALS documents, and various file attachments. Web technologies appeared, including HTML 2.0 and form-based file upload. Routing and operations tools like Route Servers, subnet management, and operational statistics were documented. Network infrastructure work covered remote procedure calls, WHOIS directories, and various specialized protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: The main focus was the next version of IP and keeping communications secure. Email got new features for attachments and status reporting. The World Wide Web was being standardized too.

sections.title: Standards Track and Informational Documents
sections.content:
The 100 RFCs in this range had different statuses. Many were marked [STANDARDS-TRACK], indicating they were being evaluated for adoption as Internet standards. Examples include RTP (RFC 1889), SMTP extensions (RFCs 1869, 1870, 1891), IPv6 (RFC 1883), and DNS extensions for IPv6 (RFC 1886). Others were labeled Experimental, meaning they were proposals for testing and evaluation. Many were marked Informational, providing guidance or documentation of systems and practices rather than protocols for standardization.

The memo explicitly noted that standards-track documents could change status during the approval process, so readers should consult the current standards document for authoritative status information rather than relying on the labels in RFC 1899 itself.
sections.plainLanguage: Some RFCs were being groomed to become official standards. Others were experiments or reference guides. The memo told readers to check the official status list if they needed to know for sure.

sections.title: Notable RFCs in This Range
sections.content: Several documents from this range became cornerstones of the Internet. RFC 1883, the IPv6 specification, defined the next-generation Internet Protocol that is gradually replacing IPv4. RFC 1889 and 1890 defined RTP and its audio-video profile, foundational for real-time media on the Internet. RFC 1831-1833 standardized the Remote Procedure Call (RPC) protocol and related data serialization, essential infrastructure for distributed systems. RFC 1866 standardized HTML 2.0, fixing the then-emerging web language. RFC 1869 and 1891 extended SMTP with service advertising and delivery status notifications, essential for reliable email. RFC 1825-1827 defined the IP security architecture and protocols that underpin encrypted communications. RFC 1898, the CyberCash protocol, documented one of the first working Internet payment systems.
sections.plainLanguage: Some standouts: the spec for the next Internet, protocols for video calls, how to make secure connections, a standard for web pages, and an early payment system.

sections.title: Use as a Reference
sections.content:
RFC 1899 serves as a historical reference, a finding aid, and a statement of the state of Internet work during the mid-1990s. Readers looking for a specific topic or protocol could scan the index to find the relevant RFC number and then fetch the full document. The brief descriptions helped readers decide whether an RFC was worth reading in full. For historians and researchers, the index provides a snapshot of where the Internet standards effort was focused at a moment of rapid change.

Similar summary RFCs have been published for other ranges, forming a chronological index of the entire RFC series.
sections.plainLanguage: It's a finding tool. If you wanted to learn about a topic, you looked it up here and got pointed to the right RFC.

references.text: Reynolds, J.K. and Postel, J., "Assigned Numbers", STD 2, RFC 1700, October 1994.
